consensus_summary: Justification is God's forensic declaration that a sinner is righteous — acquittal from condemnation and right standing with God — grounded in Christ's atoning work and received by faith apart from works of the law, classically involving the imputation of Christ's righteousness; recognized alternatives include the transformative Catholic view, the covenantal New Perspective, and a demonstrative/vindication sense (James 2, Matt 11:19).
book_summary: To justify is, generically, to judge, declare, or demonstrate a person, word, deed, or cause right against a question or charge — the opposite of condemnation. God answers the charge against the sinner by grace through Christ, forgiving sin rather than 'renaming ungodliness righteousness'; works may vindicate a claimed faith but cannot purchase mercy or put God in debt.
consensus_core_identification: A soteriological, forensic verdict: God declares the believing sinner righteous through Christ, typically with imputed righteousness.
book_core_identification: A general judicial/vindicatory act — declaring or demonstrating right against a charge (opposite of condemning) — of which God's gracious, forgiving acquittal of the sinner through Christ is the central soteriological instance, and vindication of faith by works a legitimate secondary use.
boundary_disagreement: The book widens the term beyond the soteriological courtroom verdict to cover all judicial and demonstrative uses (human judges justifying the righteous, Deut 25:1; wisdom justified of her children, Matt 11:19; the people justifying God, Luke 7:29; Abraham and Rahab justified by works, Jas 2). It also presses a boundary within the soteriological sense: justification is God forgiving and covering sin (Rom 4:7-8), pointedly not 'renaming ungodliness righteousness,' which implicitly qualifies or resists the classic imputed-alien-righteousness formulation that the consensus and the book's own common-view note treat as standard.
rationale: The book keeps the consensus's central referent — a legal declaration of righteousness opposed to condemnation, granted by God's grace through Christ and received by faith, not purchasable by works — so there is no replacement of the core. But it materially changes the term's extension by defining it lexically (any declaration/demonstration of rightness against a charge), folding in the demonstrative and general-judicial senses that the consensus lists only as alternatives, and by fully affirming James's justification-by-works as vindication of faith alongside Paul. The phrase 'forgiving rather than renaming ungodliness righteousness' (echoing Prov 17:15) marks a real boundary dispute with the imputation mechanics of the common Protestant view, but framed as clarification (justification as pardon of the ungodly, Rom 4:5-8), not as denial that God graciously acquits believers. That is refinement at the boundary, not contradiction of the core.
strongest_objection: One could argue the book's remark that God forgives 'rather than renaming ungodliness righteousness,' combined with Proverbs 17:15 (justifying the wicked is abomination), amounts to a rejection of the imputation of Christ's righteousness — the very mechanism the primary consensus reading names — and thus contradicts rather than refines it. However, since the consensus itself flags the mechanism as contested (Responses B and C mark no settled consensus) and the book retains gracious forensic acquittal by faith apart from works, this is best read as a boundary dispute within a shared core rather than a replaced referent.
